newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Obstacles seen in Budapest bourse bull run.
newsitem.headline: Obstacles seen in Budapest bourse bull run.

text.p: Hungarian stocks have hit successive highs on one of the few eastern European bourses tracking Wall Street but analysts see obstacles to Budapest extending a run which has seen it more than double this year.
On Tuesday the BUX index closed at 3,692.06 points, up 9.99 points on the day, and 130 percent up on the start of the year, making Budapest one of the fastest growing world exchanges.
Unlike some others in the region where local factors and low volume dominate, Budapest has tended to follow international trends set by Wall Street and major European bourses.

"When Wall Street is going up, Americans put money into mutual funds and when the mutual funds have more money, they put it into other markets, including Budapest," said Frances Cloud, analyst at Nomura Equity Research in London.
Over the past week Budapest has mirrored the Wall Street records and local analysts were on Wednesday predicting it would extend Tuesday's gain or at least consolidate at these levels.
"I expect the market to consolidate today," said Geza Rainer of Bank Austria-GiroCredit. "In the near future third-quarter corporate results will influence prices."
But Attila Hunyadi of Buda-Cash Brokerhaz sees chemical companies Borsodchem and TVK leading the BUX higher: "I expect the market to extend its recent gains."
For the time being the market is benefiting from good corporate results -- a new batch of which are expected late this month -- and Hungary's good image among foreign investors.
In London, however, Cloud said she saw Budapest as fully valued and said expected a downward correction later this year.
Problems could also be on the horizon if the political row over the Hungarian privatisation process spilled over into the stock market and eroded western investor confidence.

The state privatisation agency APV's directors as well as the minister responsible for privatisation were dismissed earlier this month in a scandal over irregular payments of millions of dollars to an adviser.

"It may be that problems being seen on the domestic scene, particularly the problems within the government coalition because of the APV scandal might have the effect of persuading people to take some money out of Hungary," Cloud said. "But at the moment there is no sign of it."
Nathan West, salesman at Daiwa Europe Ltd's central European desk in London, said the privatisation spat was the kind of row investors had to take in their stride.
"These things do tend to blow up occasionally in East European countries and people are a little bit acclimatised to it," said West. "They are not necessarily scared off."
He too sees more steam in the Budapest bull run.
"The Hungarian market still looks reasonably good value... We've got the target for the year-end for Hungary of putting in excess of 3,900 (points)," said West.
On Tuesday December BUX index futures closed at 3,775 points, up 2.00.
"There's still a bit of euphoria that these markets have still got some way to go," West said.
"It seems that the fundamentals of the market and international sentiment are actually outweighing any sort of domestic political worries," he added.
